prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening a new regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean case of an instrument-driven advance that changes what can be measured and how accurately. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes Doppler and recoil shifts while retaining thousands of atoms, and Ye's strontium clocks and many-body clock work took the uncertainty to the 10^-18 level, roughly two orders beyond the caesium standard. The result has been confirmed independently at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE and in more than one species, the interpretation is stable, and it feeds directly into tests of relativity and constancy of constants, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches and the roadmap toward redefining the second. Four of eight members put it first, and the two credited names map onto two distinct, decisive contributions (concept and record performance), which gives a configuration that is easy to defend without an arbitrary cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and credit: the frequency-comb prize (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and the ion-clock/quantum-control prize (Wineland, 2012) already sit in the same neighbourhood, so critics can say this is a third prize for precision spectroscopy, and clock groups at NIST, JILA (Ludlow, Hinkley and others), PTB and elsewhere contributed essential steps that two names cannot cover. A second reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so one can argue the impact is prospective. I think the first is a presentational point because the lattice-clock concept is a distinct invention, and the second is not needed for a prize about a demonstrated measurement capability, but neither can be dismissed entirely.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube/Halzen first as the opening of a new observational window, and ranks the clocks second as a clear, mature pair of decisive contributors.
responses.response: I accept that neutrino astronomy is a real discovery of something new in nature, and I agree with Pearce that Katori and Ye are the unambiguous decisive pair. Where I differ is on B027: the credited list gives only Halzen for a large collaboration project, so a single-name prize would sit awkwardly with the instrument builders and early proposers, and source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still at moderate significance. The clocks have no comparable attribution gap and no maturity gap, so I would keep B027 as a candidate for a later year rather than this one.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED (Blais, Schoelkopf, Wallraff) first because it is the architecture of essentially all superconducting processors, and notes that the 2025 prize covered macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of circuit QED, and Johansson is right that it is mature. My reservation is the timing and attribution that he himself flags: coming straight after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits invites the charge of returning to the same area, and the four credited names leave Girvin's role in the 2004 theory unresolved. The clocks put a sharper, independently confirmed measurement result on the table, with no recent prize in the same specific area. I would keep B003 as a strong later option, not the lead this year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a concrete prediction followed by a decisive experiment that opened moire quantum matter, while noting that attribution beyond the lead group is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by Jarillo-Herrero's experiment is a clean theory-experiment story and has had wide influence. My qualification is maturity and attribution, which Danielsson partly concedes: the pairing mechanism of the superconducting phase is still debated, the first author (Cao) and other groups are outside the credited names, and about eight years is short compared with clocks that have been confirmed in several national laboratories. If the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize this year I would not object, which is why I keep B017 as an alternative, but I do not think it is more secure than B001.

responses.point: Mehlig also ranks the lattice clock first, as a clear and original measurement advance, and treats Ye's earlier frequency-comb overlap as a presentational matter, while ranking quantum simulation with cold atoms second.
responses.response: I agree with Mehlig on the overlap point. Ye's role in the clock is distinct from the comb work recognised in 2005, and I would phrase the citation around the lattice clock to make that explicit. On quantum simulation, I share his view that it is mature as a technique but still developing as a science, and I also note that a three-person cut from five credited names (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac, Zoller) forces a choice between theory and experiment that Mehlig and Lindroth resolved differently. That unresolved allocation is why I rank B042 behind B001, even though I place it highly.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, followed by dynamical mean-field theory and tunnel magnetoresistance, and does not rank the clocks.
responses.response: I can see the logic of a condensed-matter focus, and his TMR argument about interface physics and device impact is a serious one. However, TMR follows closely on the 2007 GMR prize and its credit is contested (Yuasa and the coherent-tunnelling theorists), and he himself notes that a methods prize like DMFT is judged against discoveries it enabled. I would ask him whether the unresolved attribution questions in his top choices weigh as much as the overlap concerns raised against the clocks, since the clock configuration seems to me the cleaner of the two.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is comfortable with a third prize in precision laser spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012, or prefers to rotate to another subfield.
Whether two names are enough credit for lattice clocks given the contributions of other clock groups at NIST, JILA, PTB and RIKEN, and how the citation should be worded to reflect that.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a condition for timing or only as supporting context.
statement.conflict_note: A possible, modest connection: my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye's work grows out of the JILA frequency-comb and laser-stabilisation tradition associated with Hall; I also work in laser stabilisation and precision optical spectroscopy, and have European quantum-memory collaborations and Lund colleagues (Rippe, Walther, Kinos) who are not candidates here. The provided profile documents no direct collaboration, supervision or institutional tie with Katori or Ye, so no specific conflict is apparent, but I flag the Hall-lab link for the committee's recusal judgement.
